title: Private chef services for family offices: a complete guide
body_markdown:
Family-office private chef support is the coordination of household cooking through a clear brief, agreed responsibilities and an authorised contact, with the aim of keeping meals consistent without making the principal manage each visit. When appointing a private chef for family offices, separate recurring household meals from entertaining, then compare proposals against the same operational requirements.


**TL;DR**

- Choose a private chef for family offices by comparing household requirements, responsibilities and approval processes—not menus alone.
- myCHEF suits family offices seeking vetted chefs for household cooking, with separate support for dinner parties and catering.
- Separate recurring meals from private dining, even when both take place in the same residence.
- Confirm groceries, equipment, staffing, dietary instructions and kitchen handover before approving a proposal.


For an initial enquiry, use the [myCHEF contact page](https://www.mychef.ae/contact) to describe the residence, cooking schedule and service required. This guide explains how to prepare that brief and assess the response; it is not a household rate card or a substitute for an agreed scope.

## Why chef coordination matters for family offices

A family-office brief has to work for more than the person eating the meal. The principal sets preferences, an assistant approves arrangements, and household staff provide access and manage the kitchen. Your instructions should make those responsibilities explicit rather than leave the chef to resolve conflicting requests.

The distinction between household cooking and entertaining matters, too. Regular lunches, family dinners and weekly meal preparation need a repeatable routine. A celebration needs a separate discussion about guests, service, equipment and the event timetable, regardless of how few people attend.

**Choose the service around the work required, not the job title of the person booking it.** A family office arranging an isolated dinner needs a private-dining brief, not a recurring household arrangement with extra guests added informally.

## How should you brief and appoint a household chef?

### Define the household routine

Start with a shared document or spreadsheet. Record who needs meals, where cooking happens and which parts of the schedule are fixed. You do not need a complicated system; you need instructions that the assistant, household team and chef can all understand.

Separate regular requirements from occasional requests. For example, an illustrative brief might distinguish weekday family meals from a hosted dinner during a principal’s visit. Keep the dinner outside the recurring scope until its menu, staffing and timing are agreed.

Describe the desired result as well as the task. Meals cooked for immediate service require a different handover from meals prepared for later use.

- List the residences included in the enquiry.
- Identify the people receiving meals, including children and visiting relatives.
- Specify cooking days and intended serving times.
- Distinguish freshly served meals from meals prepared for later.
- Record travel periods and anticipated changes to the household routine.

### Assign approval and communication roles

Use a simple responsibility list before requesting proposals. Name the person who approves menus, the person who authorises additional work and the person who gives access to the property. One person can hold several roles, but each responsibility still needs an owner.

A family office should also decide what information the chef actually needs. Provide relevant food preferences and access instructions without circulating unrelated personal schedules or household documents. Ask how the provider handles confidential information; do not assume a particular confidentiality agreement applies.

Keep operational instructions in one agreed channel. Conflicting messages from a principal, assistant and house manager create an avoidable approval problem.

- Name the main operational contact and a backup.
- Identify who can approve menus and changes to scope.
- Specify how urgent changes should be communicated.
- Request the provider’s confidentiality arrangements for review.
- Agree who receives proposals, confirmations and invoices.

### Match the provider to the work

Write the scope first, then assess whether a service provider or a directly employed chef fits it. A recurring visiting arrangement suits defined cooking sessions. Direct employment is a different staffing decision, with recruitment and employment responsibilities that need separate consideration.

**myCHEF is best suited to family offices seeking vetted chefs for household cooking and separate event catering.** Its stated services include home-cooked meals, weekly meal preparation, dinner parties and corporate events. That range does not establish dedicated staffing, substitute-chef cover or a particular booking arrangement; ask for those details where they matter.

Use your brief to assess the proposed service rather than treating a broad service description as a commitment. The written proposal should identify what the provider is accepting responsibility for.

- Describe whether the requirement is recurring cooking or a single occasion.
- Ask how the proposed chef is selected for the household brief.
- Request relevant information about the provider’s vetting process.
- Confirm whether continuity of chef is part of the proposal.
- Ask how absence, schedule changes and replacement requests are handled.

### Document dietary needs and menu approval

Build a household food brief manually before discussing sample menus. Separate allergies, religious requirements, medical instructions and preferences. A disliked ingredient is not the same operational issue as an allergy, and neither should be buried in a general description such as healthy family food.

Where a household member follows clinical dietary advice, provide the relevant written instructions from their qualified clinician or dietitian. A chef enquiry should establish whether those instructions can be followed, not ask the chef to diagnose a condition or prescribe treatment.

A sample menu helps test understanding. Label it as a proposal and resolve substitutions before cooking begins.

- Record allergies separately from preferences and dislikes.
- Specify halal requirements and any ingredient restrictions.
- Identify different portions or dishes required for children.
- Agree who approves menus and ingredient substitutions.
- Ask how the kitchen setup affects the handling of dietary requirements.
- Specify how prepared meals should be identified at handover.

### Confirm kitchen access and purchasing responsibilities

Begin with a kitchen inventory and access checklist. Record the appliances, cookware, storage and serving equipment available at the residence. Ask the provider to identify gaps against the proposed menu rather than assuming a domestic kitchen can support every cooking or service format.

The guide to [groceries and equipment for private chef visits](https://www.mychef.ae/blog/do-private-chefs-in-dubai-bring-their-own-groceries-and-equipment) addresses a useful next question. For your own arrangement, put the answer in the proposal: who purchases ingredients, who approves substitutions and what equipment arrives with the chef.

Dubai access arrangements belong in the brief as practical questions. Ask the building or community team about visitor entry, deliveries, parking and any restrictions relevant to the residence.

- Share an accurate appliance and cookware inventory.
- Identify fridge, freezer and dry-storage space for the work.
- Confirm who buys ingredients and keeps purchasing records.
- Agree entry, parking and delivery arrangements with the property team.
- Define washing-up, waste handling and kitchen handover responsibilities.

### Compare the proposal and agree the handover

Use the same checklist for every proposal. Comparing a chef-only arrangement with one that includes purchasing, serving staff and equipment tells you little unless you separate those components. Ask for inclusions, exclusions and the process for approving extra work in writing.

For a myCHEF private chef enquiry, send the completed household brief and ask for a response against those requirements. The useful shortcut is a clearly scoped service proposal, not skipping the household decisions that only your office can make.

An initial agreed service gives you an opportunity to assess the arrangement against observable requirements. Review the food brief, timing, communication and kitchen handover—not just whether everyone enjoyed the menu.

- Check cooking, purchasing and service responsibilities separately.
- Record exclusions, additional-work approvals and applicable booking terms.
- Confirm the agreed kitchen handover standard.
- Ask for storage and reheating instructions where meals are prepared ahead.
- Review the service with the household contact before changing the routine.

## Which service format fits the household?

The strongest proposal is the one that matches the actual work. Use this comparison to distinguish household support from employment and event services; it is not a ranking of providers.

| Option | Best for | Main advantage | Key limitation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Recurring visiting chef | Households needing scheduled cooking sessions | Organises cooking around an agreed routine | Work outside the agreed visits needs separate confirmation |
| Weekly meal preparation | Households needing meals ready for later | Separates cooking time from mealtimes | Requires agreed storage, identification and reheating arrangements |
| Directly employed household chef | Households seeking an employed culinary role | Allows the household to define an ongoing role | Adds recruitment, employment and staff-management responsibilities |
| Private dining | A single hosted meal or dinner party | Builds the menu and service around one occasion | Does not establish a recurring household cooking arrangement |
| Event catering | Celebrations or business events | Addresses guest service and event logistics | Event scope does not automatically include everyday household meals |

Do not treat these formats as interchangeable. A visiting chef’s cooking brief does not automatically include table service, and a catered dinner does not establish an ongoing household schedule.


![Comparison of recurring household cooking formats with private dining and event catering](https://media.get-ryze.ai/workspace-article-images-public/c051e50c-247c-4cc9-9172-c17e3f824fb9/body-38ae5d775925d202b730e3a89da7c732.jpg)

*Recurring cooking and entertaining need separate scopes, even at the same residence.*


## What should the proposal include and exclude?

Read the scope before comparing the total. Menu complexity, cooking frequency, purchasing responsibilities, service staff, equipment and work across different residences are all items to clarify. Ask the provider to explain how each affects the proposal rather than assuming the same terms apply to every household.

A useful proposal distinguishes **food preparation**, **guest service** and **household coordination**. Cooking dinner does not by itself establish who lays the table, serves courses, clears glassware or manages suppliers.

Check these boundaries explicitly:

- **Ingredients:** Who selects, purchases, transports and approves substitutions?
- **Staffing:** Is the proposal for cooking only, or does it include service staff?
- **Equipment:** What must the household provide, and what is supplied separately?
- **Handover:** What cleaning, meal labelling and storage instructions are included?
- **Changes:** What terms apply when dates, menus, locations or guest numbers change?

Use the current written proposal for the actual commercial terms. Do not turn an earlier household quotation into a standing assumption for a different residence or occasion.

## Common mistakes family offices make

### Treating every residence as the same kitchen

A menu agreed for one property is not a complete operational brief for another. Check equipment, storage, access and the household contact at each residence before extending the arrangement.

### Allowing several people to change the brief independently

A principal’s preference, a guest request and an assistant’s instruction need a clear route to approval. Keep a current version of the brief and identify who can authorise changes.

### Folding entertaining into the household routine

A dinner party introduces guest service and event timing, even in the family dining room. Request a separate scope rather than assuming regular meal preparation covers the occasion.

### Assuming privacy terms without reviewing them

Discretion is an expectation, not a substitute for agreed terms. Ask about confidentiality, photography, information sharing and access to household instructions before approving the service.

### Assessing the meal but ignoring the handover

A successful arrangement also needs clear storage instructions, an agreed kitchen condition and useful communication with household staff. Include those points in your review rather than leaving them as unspoken expectations.

## FAQ


**What should a family office send when enquiring about a private chef?**

Send the residence location, intended cooking dates or frequency, household meal requirements and service required. Include dietary instructions, kitchen details and the name of the person authorised to approve the scope.

**Is a recurring private chef the same as a live-in chef?**

No. Recurring cooking visits and a live-in employment arrangement are different scopes. Confirm the working pattern, responsibilities and contractual arrangement rather than relying on the phrase private chef.

**Can myCHEF help with family meals and a separate dinner party?**

myCHEF provides household cooking, weekly meal preparation, dinner parties and catering. Brief recurring meals and the dinner party separately so each proposal addresses the appropriate food, staffing and practical requirements.

**Does hiring a private chef include groceries and kitchen cleaning?**

Groceries and kitchen cleaning must be confirmed in the individual proposal. Specify purchasing, ingredient approvals, washing-up, waste handling and the expected handover condition before agreeing the service.

**How should a family office handle allergies and dietary instructions?**

Provide a written brief that distinguishes allergies, medical instructions, religious requirements and preferences. Ask the provider to confirm what can be accommodated in the proposed kitchen and service arrangement.

**Can the same chef work across different residences?**

Work across residences requires explicit confirmation from the provider. Share each location, its kitchen facilities, access arrangements and the intended schedule before assuming the same arrangement applies.

**How do we compare private chef proposals fairly?**

Compare proposals against the same household brief and separate cooking, purchasing, staffing, equipment and handover responsibilities. Review exclusions and change terms alongside the proposed menu.

- [Coordinating villa concierge and recurring chef visits](https://www.mychef.ae/blog/how-to-connect-villa-concierge-to-recurring-private-chef-visits)

## Start with the household brief

The most useful document is not the sample menu. It is the agreed responsibility list: who approves, who purchases, who provides access and what the chef hands back. Set those boundaries before discussing individual dishes.

To enquire with myCHEF, send your date or intended start date, Dubai location, household or guest count, and the service required. Specify recurring household cooking, weekly meal preparation or a single hosted occasion so the enquiry starts with the right scope.


**Share your household requirements**

Include dates, location, household or guest count, dietary needs and the service required.

**[Send your brief](https://www.mychef.ae/contact)**
